items.title: L8: Reading grade, pay, contract and location signals
items.source: Civil Service Jobs adverts; GOV.UK, Civil Service grades and pay
items.body: An advert carries signals beyond the headline. The grade tells you the level of responsibility: an Administrative Officer role usually involves processing and supporting work, an Executive Officer role usually involves more independent casework or team coordination, and a Higher Executive Officer role usually involves managing people, analysis or policy tasks. Pay is shown as a range. National and London figures often differ, and a role may offer a pay band with progression through the range over time, though departments set their own rules. Check whether the figure includes allowances or is the basic salary, and whether pay changes if you work from a different location. The contract type matters. A permanent post has no end date; a fixed-term appointment ends on a stated date and may or may not be extended; a loan or secondment is for existing civil servants. A role described as 'hybrid' usually expects a share of time in an office, and the advert should state a base location or a minimum attendance. Read any wording on travel, shifts, on-call duties or weekend work. Watch for conditions such as 'must live within a commutable distance'. If the advert says that the role is 'open to external candidates', that does not mean that every candidate will be treated alike for pay on appointment, so ask the contact about starting pay if it matters to your decision.

questions.prompt: An Executive Officer advert lists 'managing a caseload with limited supervision'. What does this signal about the role?

options.text: Line management of a large team of officers
A graduate scheme with fixed rotations between teams
Mostly supervised data entry, with every decision checked
Independent work at a level above basic processing

questions.hint: Casework with limited supervision is typical of the EO level.

questions.prompt: The advert shows a London salary and a national salary. Priya will be based in Leeds. Which figure is likely to apply?

options.text: Whichever one she can agree at interview, as both are open
The average of the two, since the role covers two locations
The national figure, since the base location decides it
The London figure, because the department's head office is there

questions.hint: Pay bands usually follow the base location named in the advert.

questions.prompt: Which wording most clearly signals a fixed-term appointment?

options.text: 'This appointment is for 18 months, with a possible extension'
'Applications close at 11:55pm on the closing date'
'You will be assessed against the Civil Service Success Profiles'
'Hybrid working is available for this role'

questions.hint: Duration language shows the contract type.

questions.prompt: Hybrid working is mentioned but no attendance expectation is given. What is the sensible step?

options.text: Assume full-time office attendance, since no pattern is stated
Ask the contact how often attendance is expected and where the base is
Assume full-time home working is offered, since hybrid usually means that
Leave it until after the offer, when everything can be agreed

questions.hint: Hybrid expectations vary, so check before applying.

questions.prompt: Why is it worth checking whether a salary figure includes allowances?

options.text: Allowances are paid only to external starters, not to existing staff
Allowances are deducted from basic salary once the probation period ends
Allowances are set by the sift score of each candidate
A basic salary and a total package can differ

questions.hint: Comparing like with like needs clarity on what the figure covers.

questions.prompt: An advert is 'open to external candidates'. What can Sam not safely assume?

options.text: That the Recruitment Principles apply to the competition
That starting pay will be the same for every candidate
That the advert has a closing date and time
That anyone outside the Civil Service may apply

questions.hint: Pay on appointment can depend on rules and the candidate's situation.

questions.prompt: Which phrase in an advert most plausibly limits who can realistically apply?

options.text: 'Feedback will be given to all candidates who are interviewed'
'A full job description is attached to this advert'
'Candidates must live within a commutable distance of the office'
'Applications are welcome from all backgrounds and communities'

questions.hint: Location conditions can affect eligibility or practicality.

questions.prompt: A role mentions 'rota-based weekend working'. What should a candidate do before applying?

options.text: Check it suits their commitments and ask how much notice of rotas is given
Raise it for the first time at interview, when the panel can explain it
Assume it is optional, as no hours are stated
Treat the wording as standard text that is rarely applied in practice

questions.hint: Working patterns are a practical condition of the job.

questions.prompt: What does progression within a pay range usually depend on?

options.text: The candidate's age and length of service
A guaranteed annual rise whatever the performance
The department's own rules, not simply time passing
The candidate's score at the sift stage

questions.hint: Departments set their own progression rules.

questions.prompt: Which part of an advert best tells a candidate what the post-holder will do day to day?

options.text: The role summary and key responsibilities
The closing date section, since busy periods reveal the workload
The security clearance section, since it lists the systems used
The salary and allowances paragraph, since pay reflects the duties of the job

questions.hint: Responsibilities set out the duties.

items.title: L8: The reserve list dilemma and competing offers
items.source: Civil Service Jobs guidance; Civil Service Commission, Recruitment Principles
items.body: Candidates sometimes face a choice between an offer in hand and a possible one later. Suppose you have a conditional offer for a role you find acceptable, and you are on a reserve list for a role you prefer. The reserve list is not an offer, so it cannot be treated as one. Departments do not usually promise a date, and the list may not be reached. You have to weigh the certainty of one against the possibility of the other. A useful approach is to write down the facts: the closing date of your decision, the list's end date, how many candidates ranked above you, and what you would lose by waiting. You can ask the department holding the list whether it expects vacancies and roughly when; many will give a general indication but cannot promise. You may also ask the department with the offer for more time, though it is not obliged to extend. If you accept an offer and later get a better one, you can withdraw, but it is better to be open and early because resigning from a job you have not started can affect your standing and the resources the department has spent on checks. Do not misstate your situation to either department. Never tell one department that you have an offer you do not have in order to press the other.

questions.prompt: Jade has a conditional offer she finds acceptable and is fifth on a reserve list for a role she prefers. How should she decide?

options.text: Ask the offering department to wait for as long as it takes
Note the deadline, the list end date, her rank and the cost of waiting
Decline the offer, since a reserve list place is as good as an offer
Accept the offer and ignore the list, since reserve lists never lead to jobs

questions.hint: A reserve list is a possibility rather than an offer, so weigh the facts.

questions.prompt: Which statement about reserve lists is accurate?

options.text: They are binding offers of employment
They cannot be used once you accept another job
They guarantee a post within a month
The list may never reach every candidate on it

questions.hint: A reserve list does not guarantee a post.

questions.prompt: What question to the department holding the list is reasonable?

options.text: Which other candidates have accepted jobs elsewhere
Whether it expects vacancies and roughly when
Whether it can guarantee her a place by Friday
Whether it will raise her rank if she asks

questions.hint: Departments may indicate expectations but cannot promise.

questions.prompt: The offering department says it cannot extend Jade's decision date. What does this mean?

options.text: Her pre-employment checks are cancelled
The reserve list will move her up automatically
It must extend the date, since she has asked in writing
She must decide by that date or lose the offer

questions.hint: Departments are not obliged to extend deadlines.

questions.prompt: Which action is dishonest?

options.text: Asking how long the list will remain open
Asking for more time to decide
Telling one department she holds a firm offer elsewhere when she does not
Telling a department that another application is still in progress

questions.hint: Misstating your situation to press a department is dishonest.

questions.prompt: Why is it better to be open and early if an accepted offer might be withdrawn from by the candidate?

options.text: The department may have spent time on checks and planning
The department can claim payment from the candidate
The candidate will be barred from the Civil Service for good
The reserve list is deleted when an offer is declined

questions.hint: Early notice reduces waste and protects reputation.

questions.prompt: Marcus accepts an offer, then is contacted from a reserve list for a better role. What is the sensible next step?

options.text: Tell both departments honestly and decide quickly
Say nothing to the first and start with the second
Ask the second to hold the post while he considers
Ask the first to keep the offer open until he has started elsewhere

questions.hint: Open communication minimises harm and lets both departments plan.

questions.prompt: Why is it useful to know how many candidates rank above you on a list?

options.text: It determines which department will offer you the post first
It changes your interview score once a vacancy is confirmed
It gives a sense of whether the list will reach you
It decides the pay you will be offered if the list is reached

questions.hint: Rank position indicates whether the list may reach you.

questions.prompt: What is the biggest risk of declining a good offer to wait for a reserve list place?

options.text: The offer is withdrawn from every other candidate and given back to you
The list place is cancelled automatically once you decline anything
The department may charge a fee to candidates who decline offers
The list may never reach you, leaving you without a job

questions.hint: The list is uncertain.

questions.prompt: What can a candidate sensibly do while waiting for a list outcome?

options.text: Contact the panel every few days to ask where she now ranks
Keep applying and keep contact details current
Stop all other applications until the list has been used up
Tell other departments that she already holds an offer to speed them up

questions.hint: Keeping options open and being reachable is sensible.

items.title: L8: Judging the strength of written evidence
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles; GOV.UK, Civil Service Behaviours
items.body: Learning to judge evidence is a skill that helps you in two ways: you see the weak points of your own draft, and you understand what markers reward. Strong evidence is specific, personal, concrete and linked to a result. Specific means a real event with a context, not a general claim. Personal means that the answer shows what the writer did, not what the team did. Concrete means that details such as numbers, timeframes, people or tools appear. Linked to a result means that a change or outcome can be described, even if small. Compare 'I improved the way we handled queries' with 'I noticed repeated queries about opening hours, drafted a short reply template, and the number of follow-up emails fell over the next month'. The second shows the problem, the action and the outcome. Another test is substitution: if you could swap another candidate's name into your answer without changing it, it is too generic. Be careful with the tone of your answers. Humble but clear is better than boastful or vague. Avoid jargon and acronyms the marker may not know. Check whether the example actually shows the behaviour in the question: a good story about hard work may not show Changing and Improving. An answer that shows poor judgement can lose marks even if the outcome was good, for example bypassing a rule to hit a deadline.

questions.prompt: Which statement is the strongest piece of evidence?

options.text: 'I am someone who has always found better ways of working wherever I have been'
'I improved the way we handled queries, and everyone in the team benefited from the changes'
'We developed better procedures through teamwork over a long period of the year'
'I noticed repeated queries on opening hours, drafted a reply template, and follow-up emails fell'

questions.hint: It names the problem, the action and a measurable outcome.

questions.prompt: What is the substitution test?

options.text: Swapping the order of the Situation and Task
Checking whether another candidate's name could be swapped in
Replacing a weak word with a stronger one, throughout
Replacing your example with one used by a colleague

questions.hint: A generic answer fits anyone and scores low.

questions.prompt: An answer to a Changing and Improving question describes working very long hours to finish a job. What is the problem?

options.text: It shows hard work but no change that the candidate made
Long hours must never be mentioned, as they suggest poor planning
It does not contain a Situation, which every STAR answer needs
It should have been a leadership answer, since it describes managing time

questions.hint: The example must show the behaviour asked about.

questions.prompt: Which is 'concrete' evidence?

options.text: A statement that the candidate is enthusiastic about the job
A list of strengths that the candidate believes the role needs
Numbers, timeframes, tools or people involved
A quotation taken from the person specification

questions.hint: Concrete detail makes evidence checkable.

questions.prompt: A candidate hit a deadline by skipping a mandatory check and says so proudly. What is the likely effect?

options.text: The marker will treat it as a different behaviour
The marker may question judgement, even though the deadline was met
The marker will award top marks for delivering at pace
The marker will ignore the skipped check as irrelevant

questions.hint: Poor judgement can lose marks even where the outcome is good.

questions.prompt: Why avoid unexplained acronyms in an answer?

options.text: They always use up more of the word limit than the full words would
Acronyms count as spelling mistakes and lose marks automatically
The marker may not know them, so the evidence is unclear
Acronyms are banned across the Civil Service in written applications

questions.hint: Clarity helps the marker credit your evidence.

questions.prompt: Which tone is best for a behaviour answer?

options.text: Boastful, to show confidence in every detail of the work
Light and humorous, so that the answer stands out from others
Cautious and apologetic, so that no claim can be challenged
Clear and measured, saying what you did

questions.hint: Clear, humble and specific is credible.

questions.prompt: Which phrase most weakens an answer?

options.text: 'We all pitched in and it somehow got done'
'I asked the customer what they needed'
'I checked each figure against the source'
'I agreed a revised timetable with my manager'

questions.hint: Vague group language hides personal contribution.

questions.prompt: Aleena reads her draft and cannot find the result. What should she do?

options.text: Leave it, since results are optional in STAR
Cut the Action to leave room for a longer Situation
Add what changed because of her action, or pick a stronger example
Add a general remark that the work was a success

questions.hint: A result completes the evidence.

questions.prompt: Why is it sensible to have a trusted person read your draft?

options.text: They can raise your score by endorsing it
A fresh reader spots unclear or generic points you no longer see
They can choose the best example for you
They can submit it on your behalf

questions.hint: A second pair of eyes finds weak spots.

items.title: L8: Discrimination types applied to realistic cases
items.source: Equality Act 2010; EHRC, Employment statutory code of practice
items.body: Cases in recruitment rarely come labelled. To analyse them, ask four questions. First, was a person treated differently or put at a disadvantage? Second, was it connected to a protected characteristic, including one the person is only thought to have, or one a person they are associated with has? Third, was the treatment justified, which is relevant only for indirect discrimination and some age cases? Fourth, what remedies exist? Direct discrimination can arise from assumptions, such as assuming that an older candidate will not cope with new technology. Indirect discrimination arises from a rule or practice that applies to all but puts one group at a disadvantage, such as a requirement for continuous full-time service that disadvantages those with caring responsibilities, unless the employer can show it is a proportionate means of reaching a legitimate aim. Discrimination can also arise from something connected with a person's disability, where the treatment is unfavourable and not justified, and from the failure to make reasonable adjustments. Harassment need not be directed at the person who experiences it. Pregnancy and maternity protection means a candidate should not be rejected because she is pregnant, though she is not required to disclose it. Remember that bad management or an unfair decision is not necessarily discrimination; the link to a protected characteristic must be shown.

questions.prompt: A panel assumes an older candidate cannot learn new software and scores her down without asking. What is this?

options.text: Direct age discrimination based on an assumption
Discrimination arising from a disability that has not been disclosed
Victimisation, because she has asked a question about the software
Indirect discrimination caused by a neutral scoring rule

questions.hint: Treating someone worse because of age, based on a stereotype, is direct.

questions.prompt: An advert requires 'five years of unbroken full-time service'. Which group might be disadvantaged by it?

options.text: People who have worked for the Civil Service all their career, who are advantaged
Only those who hold degrees, since the rule favours long qualifications
Only those who live outside cities, who cannot attend selection events
People with caring career breaks, who might claim indirect discrimination

questions.hint: A neutral rule can disadvantage those with caring responsibilities.

questions.prompt: What must an employer show to defend indirect discrimination?

options.text: That few candidates have complained about it
That the rule is proportionate and serves a legitimate aim
That the rule has always been used in the department
That the candidates accepted it when they applied

questions.hint: Justification means proportionate and legitimate.

questions.prompt: Which is not, on its own, discrimination?

options.text: Treating a candidate worse for having supported a colleague's complaint
Rejecting a candidate because of her race or ethnic origin
Refusing an agreed adjustment without a good reason
An unfair decision with no link to a protected characteristic

questions.hint: Unfairness alone is not discrimination unless it is linked to a characteristic.

questions.prompt: A woman is rejected after the interviewer learns she is pregnant. What is the key point?

options.text: It is unlawful, and she did not have to disclose it
It is lawful if she could not start immediately, since the post was urgent
It is unlawful only if she had told the department before the interview
It is lawful, since pregnancy is not covered until a person is employed

questions.hint: Pregnancy and maternity is protected.

questions.prompt: A panel member jokes about a candidate's friend's religion, making the candidate uncomfortable. Might this be harassment?

options.text: It can be only if the candidate shares the friend's religion
It can be only if the joke was recorded in the panel notes
It can be, as harassment need not relate to the person's own characteristic
It cannot be, since the joke concerned someone who was not a candidate

questions.hint: Harassment can relate to a characteristic of someone associated with the person.

questions.prompt: Which question should be asked first when analysing a case?

options.text: What salary and grade did the advert state for the post?
Was someone treated differently or put at a disadvantage?
How long did the interview last, compared with others?
Who else applied for the post, and how did they score?

questions.hint: Start with the treatment.

questions.prompt: A candidate is refused an agreed alternative-format test and then scores badly. What is most relevant?

options.text: Victimisation
An unfair reserve list decision
The failure to make a reasonable adjustment
Indirect discrimination on the basis of age

questions.hint: The duty to adjust is separate from other kinds.

questions.prompt: Which is 'discrimination arising from disability'?

options.text: Treating every candidate in exactly the same way throughout
Giving extra time in a test so that a disabled candidate can complete it
Providing an interpreter at interview, where requested in advance
Unfavourable treatment for something arising from disability, if not justified

questions.hint: It concerns unfavourable treatment for something arising from disability.

questions.prompt: Devika thinks she was rejected because she complained last year about discrimination in another department. What might this be?

options.text: Victimisation
Direct age discrimination
A normal selection outcome
Indirect discrimination

questions.hint: Penalising someone for making a complaint can be victimisation.

items.title: L8: Positive action and what it does not allow
items.source: Equality Act 2010, sections 158 and 159; Government Equalities Office guidance
items.body: People often confuse positive action with positive discrimination. Positive discrimination, meaning giving a job to someone only because of a protected characteristic regardless of merit, is generally unlawful in the UK. Positive action is lawful in limited ways and is about helping to level the field. General positive action allows an employer to take proportionate steps where people with a protected characteristic have a disadvantage connected to it, have different needs, or participate less in an activity than others. Examples include targeted outreach, mentoring, encouraging applications from under-represented groups, and training to prepare for applications. In recruitment, there is a narrower provision sometimes called the tie-break. Where two candidates are as qualified as each other, an employer may choose the one with a protected characteristic if it reasonably thinks that group is disadvantaged or under-represented in that kind of work, and if doing so is a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim. It must not be a blanket policy, and it cannot be used to choose a weaker candidate. For the Civil Service, merit remains the rule, and any use of positive action has to be consistent with the Recruitment Principles. The Disability Confident interview offer is a different mechanism: it secures an interview for disabled applicants who meet the minimum criteria, but it does not secure the job.

questions.prompt: Which describes positive discrimination?

options.text: Choosing someone solely because of a protected characteristic, regardless of merit
Making reasonable adjustments for disabled candidates
Offering mentoring to a group that is disadvantaged
Encouraging under-represented groups to apply for vacancies

questions.hint: It breaks the merit principle and is generally unlawful.

questions.prompt: Which is an example of lawful positive action?

options.text: Rejecting all candidates from one group, to reduce their numbers
Appointing a clearly weaker candidate because of a protected characteristic
Running outreach events to encourage applications
Adding marks to one group's sift scores before ranking begins

questions.hint: Outreach and support are proportionate and lawful.

questions.prompt: When can the recruitment tie-break be used?

options.text: Whenever one candidate scores slightly lower but belongs to a protected group
When two candidates are equally qualified, a group is under-represented and it is proportionate
Whenever a hiring manager thinks a candidate from a minority group would fit well
As a standing policy applied automatically to every campaign in the department

questions.hint: The tie-break needs equal merit and proportionality.

questions.prompt: Why can the tie-break not be used to choose a weaker candidate?

options.text: Weaker candidates are never appointed in any Civil Service competition
It is available only for external vacancies, never internal ones
Candidates have no right to a reasoned decision in any case
It applies only where candidates are as qualified as each other

questions.hint: The condition is equal merit.

questions.prompt: The Disability Confident interview offer differs from the tie-break because it...

options.text: applies only to graduate entrants
changes the scores awarded at the sift
guarantees the job to disabled candidates
secures an interview if the minimum criteria are met, not the job

questions.hint: An interview offer does not decide who is appointed.

questions.prompt: A department announces that every third post must go to a woman whatever the scores. What is the issue?

options.text: It is a standard sift rule used in most departments
It is lawful positive action, since women are under-represented
It is a blanket preference that ignores merit
It is a reasonable adjustment for a disadvantaged group

questions.hint: Positive discrimination ignores merit.

questions.prompt: Which phrase best describes the Civil Service rule for appointments?

options.text: Merit, on the basis of fair and open competition
Quotas set by protected characteristic and reviewed each year
First come, first served, in order of the applications received
The line manager's choice, once the panel has produced a shortlist

questions.hint: Merit is the rule.

questions.prompt: Mentoring for staff from a group disadvantaged in progression is generally...

options.text: Always unlawful, since it favours one group
Lawful positive action, if proportionate
A form of reserve list
A kind of harassment

questions.hint: Support for disadvantaged groups can be lawful.

questions.prompt: What must an employer reasonably think before using the tie-break?

options.text: A basis of disadvantage or under-representation in that work
That the candidate scored slightly lower
That the candidate would cost less
That the candidate is popular with the panel

questions.hint: A basis in disadvantage or under-representation is required.

questions.prompt: Which is not a feature of lawful positive action?

options.text: Being aimed at a legitimate need
Being based on evidence of disadvantage
Ignoring the candidates' merit entirely
Being proportionate to the aim

questions.hint: Positive action does not ignore merit.

items.title: L8: Disclosure, privacy and what happens to your information
items.source: UK GDPR and Data Protection Act 2018; ICO guidance; GOV.UK, Disability Confident
items.body: Candidates often wonder whether to disclose a disability or health condition and what the department does with the information. You are not generally obliged to disclose a disability when you apply, although you will need to say so if you want the Disability Confident interview offer or reasonable adjustments. Departments collect equality monitoring data, which is usually kept separate from the application and not seen by the panel. Information about your health is special category data under data protection law, which means the organisation must have a lawful reason to hold it, must keep it secure, and must use it only for the purposes it gave. You have the right to know what is held about you, to ask for errors to be corrected, and in some cases to ask for deletion. A department can share information on a need-to-know basis, for instance with the people arranging a test adjustment. Before a conditional offer, health questions are restricted. After a conditional offer, an occupational health check or a health questionnaire may be used to see whether adjustments are needed, and the answers should not be used to reject someone for an unlawful reason. If you decide not to disclose, you may not get adjustments you did not request. If you change your mind, you can usually tell the department later. Keep in mind that what you provide in a security vetting form is a separate process and should be accurate.

questions.prompt: When applying, is a candidate generally obliged to disclose a disability?

options.text: Only after the offer is made in writing and accepted
Not generally, but it is needed for the interview offer or adjustments
Always, on the application form, or the application is invalid
Only if the condition is visible to the panel on the day

questions.hint: Disclosure is usually a choice.

questions.prompt: Why is equality monitoring data usually kept separate from the application?

options.text: So the hiring manager has a summary of the candidates' profiles
So the form looks longer and more thorough to applicants
So candidates can edit their answers after the closing date
So the panel cannot see it and it cannot affect scoring

questions.hint: Separation protects fairness.

questions.prompt: What does 'special category data' mean for health information?

options.text: It falls outside data protection law, because it is voluntary
It needs a lawful reason and extra care in how it is held
It can be shared freely with any employee who asks about the post
It must be published openly, so that candidates can compare it

questions.hint: Health data is more strictly protected.

questions.prompt: Which right do candidates have under data protection law?

options.text: To ask what is held and to have errors corrected
To postpone the process while they consider their position
To choose which members of staff sit on the panel
To see the scores that other candidates were given

questions.hint: Individuals have access and rectification rights.

questions.prompt: Who may see details of a test adjustment?

options.text: Everyone in the department, so that support can be shown
The other candidates, so that the process is seen to be open
Only people who need to know to arrange it
The candidate's current employer, who has a right to be informed

questions.hint: Need-to-know sharing is expected.

questions.prompt: A candidate did not request adjustments and then struggles in a test. What is the likely position?

options.text: The test will be re-run for all candidates so that nobody is disadvantaged
The score will be adjusted automatically after the test
The department must have provided adjustments anyway, since the test is standard
The department may not have known, so telling it early matters

questions.hint: Departments need to know to arrange adjustments.

questions.prompt: Can a candidate who did not disclose at application tell the department later?

options.text: Only after the first year in post, when probation has ended
Never, since the application form is final once submitted
Usually, and adjustments can be considered from then on
Only through a solicitor, as it counts as a legal change

questions.hint: Candidates can often disclose later.

questions.prompt: Why are health questions restricted before a conditional offer?

options.text: To prevent health being used unfairly in selection
To discourage candidates with conditions from applying at all
To save time at the interview, so questions can focus on the job
To protect panel members from having to hear awkward answers

questions.hint: Restrictions guard against discrimination.

questions.prompt: After a conditional offer, what is a legitimate use of a health questionnaire?

options.text: To reject candidates who report any health condition at all
To find out whether adjustments are needed
To publish the results to the candidate's future team
To fix the starting salary according to likely absence

questions.hint: It should be used to support, not exclude.

questions.prompt: What is true of a security vetting form compared with an adjustments request?

options.text: It can be skipped for internal candidates who are already cleared
It is the same process, so one form covers both purposes
It is for managers only and does not apply to junior grades
It is a separate process and the answers must be accurate

questions.hint: Vetting is separate and requires accuracy.

items.title: L8: Routes to promotion for serving civil servants
items.source: Civil Service HR guidance; Civil Service Commission, Recruitment Principles
items.body: A civil servant who wants to progress has several routes. The first is a permanent promotion by applying to an advertised vacancy at a higher grade through a fair and open competition. These adverts appear on Civil Service Jobs and may be open to current civil servants only or to all. The second is temporary promotion, where a person fills a higher post for a period. The third is a development scheme, such as a talent or leadership programme, which may select people through assessment and give structured experience, though promotion at the end is not automatic. The fourth is a move between departments or professions to gain experience that makes you competitive. Some professions, such as digital, data or finance, have their own frameworks that describe skills at each grade, and these help you plan what evidence to build. Another route is a regrading of your current role, where the duties have grown significantly; this follows job evaluation and is not the same as being promoted into a different job. Applicants should ask their manager for stretch tasks, keep a record of achievements, and seek feedback. Apply when you can show the criteria for the higher grade, which is not the same as having been in post a certain number of years. Time served does not on its own earn a promotion, and an application must still be assessed on merit.

questions.prompt: Which route to a permanent promotion follows the Recruitment Principles?

options.text: Asking HR to move you up a grade once you feel ready
Applying to an advertised higher vacancy and winning a fair competition
Being given the job by a line manager who values the work
Waiting until enough years have passed in the current grade

questions.hint: Permanent promotion is through merit-based competition.

questions.prompt: Which statement about a development scheme is accurate?

options.text: It replaces the Recruitment Principles for those who are on it
It is open only to new entrants and cannot be joined by serving staff
It gives structured experience, but promotion at the end is not automatic
It guarantees promotion at the end of the scheme for everyone who completes it

questions.hint: Schemes support progression without guaranteeing it.

questions.prompt: A civil servant's duties have grown significantly. Which route addresses this?

options.text: A regrading through job evaluation, which differs from promotion
A fresh sift for the post by the Civil Service Commission
An automatic promotion to the next grade once the duties have grown
A place on a reserve list for the higher-graded post

questions.hint: Regrading is based on the weight of the job.

questions.prompt: Why might a move to a different department help later promotion?

options.text: It removes the need to show evidence in later applications
It guarantees a higher grade on return to the original department
It resets your pay to the minimum of the range, so promotion is cheaper
It provides experience and evidence that make you more competitive

questions.hint: Breadth builds evidence.

questions.prompt: When is it sensible to apply for a higher grade?

options.text: Only once your manager nominates you
Only after a secondment
When you can show the criteria for that grade with evidence
When you have reached a certain number of years in post

questions.hint: Evidence of criteria matters more than time.

questions.prompt: Why do professions publish skills frameworks?

options.text: They set the pay for each profession across all departments
They describe expected skills at each grade, so people can plan evidence
They provide the reserve lists used by each profession
They replace the behaviours in Success Profiles for specialist posts

questions.hint: Frameworks guide development.

questions.prompt: Which habit helps someone seeking promotion?

options.text: Keeping a record of achievements and seeking feedback
Keeping achievements private until an interview
Avoiding new tasks that might go wrong
Applying to every vacancy at once

questions.hint: Records and feedback support evidence.

questions.prompt: Which statement about time served is correct?

options.text: It replaces the sift
It guarantees promotion after a set number of years
It decides the pay on promotion
It does not on its own earn a promotion

questions.hint: Merit, not time, decides.

questions.prompt: An advert says 'open to Civil Servants only'. What is the position for current staff?

options.text: They skip the sift and are interviewed straight away
They apply and are assessed on merit like any other candidate
They need no evidence, since the department already knows their work
They are appointed automatically if they meet the minimum criteria

questions.hint: Merit applies.

questions.prompt: Which is a feature of temporary promotion, compared with permanent promotion?

options.text: It must be at a lower grade than the person's current one
It cannot involve any higher pay, as the post is not permanent
It lasts a limited period and does not itself confer a permanent post
It becomes permanent automatically after six months in the role

questions.hint: Temporary is time-limited.

items.title: L8: Resigning, notice and counter-offers
items.source: GOV.UK, Redundancy, dismissal and notice guidance; ACAS guidance on resigning
items.body: Once you have an unconditional offer, the next steps need care. Check your contract for the notice period, which may be a week, a month or longer. Statutory minimum notice for employees with enough service can apply, and the contract may require more. Give notice in writing, state the last day, and keep a copy. Ask your employer how any outstanding holiday will be handled; you may be paid for untaken statutory holiday, or asked to take it during the notice period. Your employer may make a counter-offer, such as more pay or a new role. Think about why you wanted to leave. A counter-offer rarely changes the reasons, such as limited progression or culture. If you accept it, you should tell the Civil Service department promptly, and recognise that you may have affected your standing with them. If you decide to leave, stay professional and complete handover tasks, because you may need a reference or want to return later. Your new department will usually agree a start date that fits your notice. If your notice is long, it is reasonable to ask if some of it can be shortened by agreement with your employer. A final point: do not take confidential material from your old employer to use at the new one, and do not tell colleagues about a new job before you have told your manager, if you can avoid it.

questions.prompt: When should Naomi hand in her notice?

options.text: On the first day of her new role, so no time is lost
After she is shortlisted, so the department can see her availability
As soon as she applies, to show commitment to the Civil Service
Once she holds an unconditional offer, following her contract's terms

questions.hint: An unconditional offer removes the risk.

questions.prompt: Which statement about notice is correct?

options.text: The contract sets it, and it may exceed the statutory minimum
It is always one week, whatever the contract says
It is not required for civil servants, who can leave at once
It is set by the new employer to suit its start date

questions.hint: Check the contract.

questions.prompt: Naomi's employer offers more pay if she stays. What is a sensible response?

options.text: Ignore it and say nothing, so as not to upset her manager
Think about why she wanted to leave, as a counter-offer rarely changes that
Accept at once, since more pay solves whatever the problem was
Tell the new department that her employer is putting pressure on her

questions.hint: Counter-offers seldom change underlying reasons.

questions.prompt: Naomi accepts the counter-offer after accepting the Civil Service offer. What should she do?

options.text: Tell the department promptly and honestly
Ask the department to hold the offer until she changes her mind again
Tell the department that the offer was withdrawn by them
Say nothing and not turn up

questions.hint: Early honest notice limits harm.

questions.prompt: How should notice be given?

options.text: Verbally to a colleague in the corridor
By text message to a friend
On a work chat channel visible to the team
In writing, with the last day stated and a copy kept

questions.hint: Writing gives a clear record.

questions.prompt: Why complete handover tasks properly?

options.text: It shortens the notice period by an agreed number of days
It raises her pay in her last month of employment
She may need a reference later, or want to return
It is required for tax purposes on her final payslip

questions.hint: Professional conduct protects your reputation.

questions.prompt: Which action is inappropriate when leaving?

options.text: Handing over files and contacts to the person who will cover
Taking confidential material to use at the new employer
Clearing her desk and returning equipment on the last day
Telling her manager before she tells her colleagues

questions.hint: Confidential material belongs to the employer.

questions.prompt: Naomi's notice is three months. What is reasonable?

options.text: Ask whether some can be shortened, accepting the employer may refuse
Hide the offer from her employer until the last week
Leave after one week regardless of the contract
Ask the new department to pay her old employer

questions.hint: Employers may agree to release earlier, but need not.

questions.prompt: What happens to untaken holiday on leaving?

options.text: It is always lost, since leaving ends all entitlement to holiday
It transfers to the new employer automatically on the start date
It is doubled to compensate for the shorter notice served
It may be paid or taken during notice, depending on the arrangements

questions.hint: Check how it is handled.

questions.prompt: Whom should Naomi usually tell first about her new job?

options.text: Her social media followers
Her colleagues, so they hear it from her
Her manager, before colleagues, where possible
Her clients, so they can plan

questions.hint: Telling the manager first is courteous.

items.title: L8: Impartiality and confidentiality in internal competitions
items.source: Civil Service Code; Civil Service Commission, Recruitment Principles
items.body: The Civil Service Code sets out four core values: integrity, honesty, objectivity and impartiality. In an internal competition they have practical effects. Integrity means not misusing your position or information. If you work in HR or a team that sees applications, you must not share information about other candidates or use it for your own advantage. Honesty means giving accurate information about your experience. Objectivity means making decisions on evidence. Impartiality means acting fairly, without favour. Suppose a colleague works on a team's workforce plan and knows that a post will be advertised soon. Telling a friend privately before the advert goes out would undermine open competition. Using confidential knowledge, such as another candidate's performance rating, to challenge them would be a misuse of information. If you are asked to sit on a panel for a post to which a colleague has applied, you should declare the relationship. An internal candidate is entitled to the same quality of process as an external one, including feedback. Managers should avoid giving favourable references only to preferred candidates, and should avoid pressure on staff either to apply or not to apply. If you are concerned about a breach of these values, you can raise it with your line manager, a nominated officer or HR, and if unresolved, take it to the Civil Service Commission.

questions.prompt: Which are the four core values of the Civil Service Code?

options.text: Merit, rank, seniority and service, as in the Recruitment Principles
Speed, value, loyalty and growth, which are set by each department
Teamwork, creativity, resilience and trust, as in the Behaviours
Integrity, honesty, objectivity and impartiality

questions.hint: These are the Code's values.

questions.prompt: A colleague in workforce planning tells a friend that a post will be advertised before the advert goes live. Why is this a problem?

options.text: It is allowed if the friend is more senior than the person who told them
It gives one person an advantage and undermines open competition
It is not a problem, since the post is internal and will be advertised anyway
It saves time, because the friend can prepare early for the advert

questions.hint: Advance information breaches fairness.

questions.prompt: Which action is a misuse of confidential information?

options.text: Using another candidate's rating from HR records to challenge them
Reading the public advert and attached job description
Asking the named contact a question about the role
Using her own appraisal to support her application

questions.hint: Misusing records breaches integrity.

questions.prompt: A colleague applies for a post you are asked to help assess. What should you do?

options.text: Warn the colleague about the questions
Say nothing and score honestly
Declare the relationship and let the department decide whether you step aside
Score the colleague lowest to avoid bias

questions.hint: Declaration lets the department manage it.

questions.prompt: What should an internal candidate expect from the process?

options.text: Little or no feedback, since managers already know how internal candidates perform
Feedback only if they are successful, as a form of induction
Feedback only through their line manager, never from the panel
The same quality of process and feedback as an external candidate

questions.hint: Equal treatment is expected.

questions.prompt: Which manager behaviour is improper?

options.text: Pressuring staff either to apply or not to apply for a post
Explaining how the process works to members of the team
Declaring a relationship with a candidate before shortlisting
Giving an accurate reference to any member of staff who asks

questions.hint: Pressure undermines fair competition.

questions.prompt: Where can concerns about a breach be raised first?

options.text: To the other candidates directly, as they are affected
With a line manager, nominated officer or HR
On social media, so other candidates can add their experiences
To the press, since internal routes are slow

questions.hint: Internal routes come first.

questions.prompt: What does objectivity require of a panel member?

options.text: Following the chair's hunch where scores are close
Choosing the candidate whose application arrived first
Deciding on evidence rather than preference
Choosing the candidate the panel finds most likeable

questions.hint: Objectivity is evidence-based.

questions.prompt: Which statement about HR staff who see applications is correct?

options.text: They must not share or use candidate information for personal advantage
They may tell managers which candidates are internal before shortlisting
They may share it with friends who are applying, if it is not marked secret
They may edit scores that look too low, to correct for harsh markers

questions.hint: Integrity applies.

questions.prompt: If concerns are unresolved internally, where may they go next?

options.text: The trade union of the candidate concerned
The Civil Service Commission
A national newspaper that covers government
The pay review body for the grade

questions.hint: The Code names the Commission as a route.

items.title: L8: Pay on appointment, promotion and level transfer
items.source: Civil Service Jobs guidance; Civil Service HR pay guidance
items.body: Pay is not always the same as the advertised range. The range shows the minimum and maximum for the grade, but the starting salary depends on departmental rules and the circumstances of the appointment. External appointees are usually appointed at or near the minimum, although departments may have limited discretion in some situations. For existing civil servants, the position differs. On promotion, pay usually increases to at least the minimum of the new grade, and departments often apply rules on the size of the increase. On a level transfer, the person's pay is usually kept the same as before, so long as it sits within the range for the new post. On a loan or secondment, the terms depend on the agreement, and allowances may differ. A temporary promotion may carry a temporary allowance rather than a permanent change. Pay may also include London or other location elements. Departments tend not to negotiate salaries, though a few may in specific circumstances. It is worth asking about pay progression, such as how long it takes to reach the top of the range, whether progression is automatic or linked to performance, and when the annual pay award is applied. Remember that pension and leave are part of the overall package and the Civil Service pension is a significant benefit. Compare the whole package, not only salary.

questions.prompt: Where are external appointees usually placed within the pay range?

options.text: Wherever they choose, as the range is open
In the middle, as a starting compromise
At or near the minimum, with limited discretion in some cases
At the maximum, to attract strong candidates

questions.hint: Starting pay generally follows rules.

questions.prompt: What usually happens to pay on promotion for an existing civil servant?

options.text: It stays exactly the same until the next annual pay award
It is chosen by the candidate within the new range
It falls to the minimum of the old grade, so the move is cost-neutral
It rises to at least the minimum of the new grade, often with rules on the increase

questions.hint: Promotion moves pay into the new range.

questions.prompt: On a level transfer, what usually happens to pay?

options.text: It falls to the minimum of the range for the new post
It stays the same, if it sits within the new post's range
It is reset according to the sift score in the competition
It doubles, as a one-off recognition of the new duties

questions.hint: Level transfers usually keep pay.

questions.prompt: How is a temporary promotion often paid?

options.text: With a temporary allowance rather than a permanent change
With a permanent pay rise that is kept after the arrangement ends
With a one-off bonus and no change to monthly pay
With no change at all, since the move is not permanent

questions.hint: Temporary promotion carries temporary terms.

questions.prompt: Why compare the whole package, not only salary?

options.text: Leave is paid on top of salary at all times
Salary is not important in the Civil Service
Pension and leave are valuable parts of the offer
Packages are identical in every department

questions.hint: The package includes more than salary.

questions.prompt: Which question about progression is sensible?

options.text: Who sets the pay of the panel that will assess me?
Is the pay range negotiable if I score highly at the sift?
Which candidate earned the highest salary in the previous campaign?
Is progression automatic or linked to performance, and how long to the top?

questions.hint: Progression terms vary.

questions.prompt: Why can an advertised range mislead?

options.text: The ranges are kept secret until the offer letter is issued
The ranges shown are always out of date and never accurate
Starting pay follows departmental rules, not simply the range
The ranges are identical in every department and grade

questions.hint: Starting pay may be near the minimum.

questions.prompt: Which statement about negotiating pay is most accurate?

options.text: Departments tend not to negotiate, though a few may in specific cases
All salaries are open to negotiation once an offer has been made
Negotiation is forbidden, and any attempt ends the offer
Negotiation is decided by the interview panel, which sets pay

questions.hint: Negotiation is limited.

questions.prompt: What can differ on a loan or secondment?

options.text: Nothing, since terms are fixed nationally for all moves
Terms and allowances, which depend on the agreement
The person's employer's name, which changes on every loan
The person's grade, which changes whenever they move

questions.hint: Terms are agreed case by case.

questions.prompt: What does a London element do?

options.text: It lowers pay for staff who happen to live in London
It is paid only to external starters, not existing staff
It applies to every role whatever the base location
It sets a different pay level for roles based in London

questions.hint: Location can change pay.

items.title: L8: Changing profession or department
items.source: Civil Service Jobs; GOV.UK, Civil Service Professions and Functions
items.body: The Civil Service is organised into professions and functions, such as policy, operational delivery, digital and data, finance, analysis, project delivery, commercial, HR and communications. A person may move between them. Doing so is easier when the skills overlap. If you are an EO in operational delivery, you may have evidence of planning, customer focus and managing quality that supports a move to project delivery or policy. A role in a different profession may ask for specific technical skills or a professional qualification, in which case the Success Profiles technical element applies. Many adverts say what is essential and what can be learned in post. Read these carefully. If you need to build a skill, consider a short loan or detail, a project in your team, learning courses within the Civil Service, or professional networks. Be ready to explain why you want the change and what you bring. Your pay and grade may be the same on a level transfer, though some changes need a move to a different grade because the work differs. When moving between departments, you may find that processes, culture and systems are different, and you may have a new probation or review period, depending on the department's rules. Consider the effect on pension and service, which are normally preserved within the Civil Service. Apply with a clear statement of how your existing evidence meets the new criteria.

questions.prompt: Which move is likely to be easiest?

options.text: Between roles where skills overlap, such as operational delivery to project delivery
From any role into a specialist role that shares no skills with it
From a technical role into one with no technical content at all

questions.hint: Overlap helps.

options.text: The online application form on Civil Service Jobs
The equipment the panel will use at interview
A typing speed test that all applicants take
Specific skills or qualifications needed for the role

questions.prompt: How can someone build a skill before applying?

options.text: Asking the panel to teach the skill during the interview
A short loan, a team project, courses or networks
Copying other candidates' examples into your own application

questions.prompt: What should a candidate be ready to explain at interview for a change of profession?

options.text: Who else is applying and how they compare
What the panel members earn in their own posts
Why they want the change and what they bring

questions.hint: Motivation and fit.

questions.prompt: What can a move between departments involve?

options.text: Different systems and culture, and sometimes a new review period
Loss of the person's leave entitlement for the first year
Loss of the person's pension rights built up so far
Nothing, since every department works in exactly the same way

questions.hint: Departments differ.

questions.prompt: What usually happens to Civil Service pension and service on a move within the Civil Service?

options.text: They restart from zero, as the contract is new
They are halved to reflect the shorter service
They are lost on any move between departments
They are normally preserved

questions.hint: Service is usually continuous.

questions.prompt: Why read what is 'essential' and what can be 'learned in post'?

options.text: It decides how long the interview will last
It shows what you must already have and what the department will teach
It tells you who else applied and what their ratings were
It sets the pay range at the offer stage

questions.hint: Adverts distinguish them.

questions.prompt: Which statement about changing profession is accurate?

options.text: The change always needs a promotion before anyone may apply
Only new qualifications count towards the new criteria
Existing evidence can support it if you show how it meets the new criteria

questions.hint: Transferable evidence is valid.

questions.prompt: Which is an example of transferable evidence?

options.text: A list of hobbies and interests included in the personal profile
A friend's testimonial about your character and sense of humour
Planning and quality checking in operational delivery, used for project delivery
A holiday itinerary organised for a group of friends in another country

questions.hint: Skills transfer between professions.

questions.prompt: Why might some moves need a different grade?

options.text: The panel prefers candidates to start again at a lower grade
The pay in the new profession is always higher
The pension in the new profession differs from the old one
The work in the new profession may be at a different level

questions.hint: Work level determines grade.

items.title: L8: Turning feedback into a development plan
items.source: Civil Service Jobs guidance; Civil Service Success Profiles
items.body: Feedback is most useful when you convert it into actions. Start by collecting everything you have: your submitted answers, the scoring scale, any written feedback, and notes from the interview. Look for patterns across more than one application. If three pieces of feedback mention that you did not describe your own actions, that is a pattern to fix. Next, separate the types of issue. Some are about presentation, such as a missing result or an over-long Situation. Some are about evidence, where you lack a strong example. Some are about content, such as the wrong behaviour being shown. Some are about the stage, such as test performance. Then set specific actions. For presentation, redraft an old answer and have someone review it. For evidence, create the example: ask for a project, volunteer for a task, or look for a lead role in a group. For interview performance, practise out loud, record yourself, and ask for a mock interview. For tests, do timed practice. Agree a time frame: for example, two weeks to redraft and a month to seek an opportunity. Review progress, and update your record. Do not change everything at once, because you will not know what worked. Treat the feedback as a view from one campaign and look for consistent messages rather than reacting to a single comment. If feedback is unclear, you can write back politely to ask for clarification.

questions.prompt: What is the first step in using feedback well?

options.text: Gather your answers, the scoring scale, feedback and notes
Change everything about your approach at once
Reapply immediately to the same campaign
Delete old applications so you start fresh

questions.hint: Gather the evidence first.

questions.prompt: Three pieces of feedback say 'did not describe your own actions'. What is this?

options.text: A fault in the system that records the feedback
A pattern to fix in how she writes the Action
A coincidence that appears across unrelated campaigns
A marker error that should simply be ignored

questions.hint: Repeated feedback reveals priorities.

questions.prompt: Which feedback is about evidence rather than presentation?

options.text: 'Your answer was over the word limit for the question'
'You lacked a strong example of leading others'
'You missed out the Result of your actions'
'Your Situation took up too much of the answer'

questions.hint: Evidence issues mean you lack the example.

questions.prompt: What is a sensible action if the problem is lack of evidence?

options.text: Reuse an old story with the names and dates altered
Invent an example that looks like the behaviour asked for
Avoid that behaviour in future applications altogether
Create the example by taking on a relevant task or project

questions.hint: Build real evidence.

questions.prompt: Why not change everything at once after feedback?

options.text: You will not know what made the difference
It would take longer than the time before the next campaign
Departments disapprove of changed applications
It is against the Civil Service rules to change so much

questions.hint: Change in stages to learn.

questions.prompt: Which action helps interview performance?

options.text: Memorising the whole advert so that each answer matches it
Waiting until the next interview to see how it goes
Practising out loud, recording yourself and doing a mock interview
Reading the feedback silently, several times, before the interview

questions.hint: Practice improves delivery.

questions.prompt: Which action helps test performance?

options.text: Writing more behaviour statements for the sift
Longer reading of the Civil Service Code before each attempt
Asking for a different type of test at the next campaign
Timed practice tests

questions.hint: Timed practice builds speed.

questions.prompt: Why set a time frame for development actions?

options.text: It reduces the pay that you are offered next time
It keeps actions specific and lets you review progress
It is required by HR for any candidate who has been rejected
It guarantees that the next application will succeed

questions.hint: A plan needs dates.

questions.prompt: What can you do if feedback is unclear?

options.text: Write back politely and ask for clarification
Ignore it, since unclear feedback is not worth acting on
Post it online and ask other candidates what it means
Challenge the marker for giving poor feedback

questions.hint: Clarification is allowed.

questions.prompt: How should you treat a single odd comment in feedback?

options.text: As proof that the panel was biased against you
As an order from the department about how to write
As one view from one campaign, looking for consistent messages
As a rule to follow in every future application

questions.hint: Look for consistency.
